cases.name: doc-english-sufficient
cases.promptMarkdown:
We're a Dutch manufacturer, Class IIa device, selling into Germany among other markets.
Our EU Declaration of Conformity is in English only. Our distributor says everything
has to be translated into German for the German market. Do we need to translate the
Declaration of Conformity?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MPDG § 8(1): the manufacturer must make the EU Declaration of Conformity available "in
deutscher oder in englischer Sprache" — German OR English. English alone is compliant.
The distributor is wrong about the DoC specifically.

PASS requires:
(1) The answer is NO, the Declaration of Conformity does not need translating —
    English alone satisfies § 8(1).
(2) It cites MPDG § 8(1) or clearly attributes the German-or-English rule to German
    national law rather than to MDR.
(3) It distinguishes the DoC from information for users and patients, which under
    § 8(2) does default to German. Saying "the DoC is fine in English, but your user
    information is a different question" is the ideal answer.

FAIL if it says the DoC must be translated into German. FAIL if it agrees with the
distributor wholesale, or answers "everything must be in German" — that is the
over-application this case exists to catch, and it is the more common error.

Not required: naming other markets, or MDR Art. 19 itself.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Does the EU Declaration of Conformity need German translation for the German market?

**German market:** confirmed — product made available in Germany, so MPDG applies
**Answer:** No. For the DoC, German **or** English is sufficient — English alone is compliant. Your distributor is over-applying the rule to the DoC, but is right about the *user-facing* information.

| Item | MDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity (Art. 19(1)) | not carried here | German **or English** — English alone suffices | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |
| Information for users and patients (labelling, IFU) | not carried here | **German**, and it is a condition of supply — products may only be handed over to users/patients if met | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 1 `[verified]` |
| Same, where information is exclusively for professional users | not carried here | English or another easily understood language permitted, but only *in begründeten Fällen* **and** exclusively professional users **and** safety-related information still in German or the user's language — all three, cumulatively | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 2 `[verified]` |
| Implant information (MDR Art. 18(1)) | not carried here | **German**, no professional-user exception | MPDG § 8(3) `[verified]` |

So the split to put to your distributor: the DoC stays in English; the IFU and labelling that reach users and patients go into German unless you can stand behind all three limbs of the § 8(2) sentence 2 exception. "Everything has to be translated" is not the rule, and neither is "English is fine everywhere."

**What would change this:**
- If your Class IIa device is **implantable**, the Art. 18(1) implant information is German regardless of who the user is — § 8(3) has no exception.
- If the device reaches lay users or patients at all, the professional-user exception is unavailable and § 8(2) sentence 1 applies in full.
- Even in a valid professional-only case, **safety-related** information must still be in German (or the user's language) — the exception never reaches it.
- Separately, if you ever run a field safety corrective action in Germany, the **FSN must be written in German** (§ 73(1) `[verified]`) — that attaches to the action taken in Germany, not to where you are established, so it will apply to you as a Dutch manufacturer.

Your Dutch establishment matters elsewhere in § 73: the duty to document an FSCA and periodically review its effectiveness, and to notify FSCA completion to the competent authority and the federal higher authority, falls on parties *established in Germany* (§ 73(2) `[verified]`) — so not on you directly, though it may fall on your German importer where your authorised representative sits outside Germany.

## Limits

> This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves, MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about France, Italy or elsewhere. Your other markets will each have their own language rules. A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

graders.evidence:
Short answer: yes — translate it into German. But your distributor is overstating the rest.

## The DoC specifically

MDR 2017/745 **Article 19(4)** is the controlling provision:

> "The EU declaration of conformity shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available on the market."

So the language isn't your choice or the distributor's — it's set by each Member State where you place the device. For Germany that means German. Your English original stays the master document; the German version is a translation of it.

Note this is separate from the labelling/IFU rule (Art. 10(11) + Annex I §23), which has its own national-language determination. Germany's language requirements sit in the **MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz), § 8. I'd verify the exact wording of that section and whether it carves out anything for professional-use-only devices before you finalise — I don't have web access in this session to pull the current text, and MPDG § 8 does contain a professional-user provision that's worth reading against your device's intended user. ZLG or BfArM can confirm. But the safe and near-universal practice for the German market is a German DoC.

## Where the distributor is wrong

"Everything has to be translated" isn't right:

- **Technical documentation** — no translation obligation to German. Germany (via ZLG and the German notified bodies) accepts English technical documentation. Competent authorities can request translation of specific parts under Art. 10(14), but that's on request, not upfront.
- **QMS documentation, clinical evaluation report, PMS/PSUR** — English is fine.
- **Label and IFU** — these *do* need German, but you presumably have that already if you're shipping there.
- There's also no MDR obligation to ship a DoC in every box (unlike the Machinery Regulation). One controlled copy to the distributor, plus availability on request, satisfies it.

Your distributor's ask on the DoC is legitimately within their remit, though — Art. 14(2)(a) requires them to verify the DoC has been drawn up before making the device available, so they have a real compliance reason to want a usable copy.

## Practical suggestion

Issue a **bilingual EN/DE DoC as a single document** rather than two separate ones. That way:

- One document number, one version, one signature — no drift between language versions
- Your Art. 14(2) verification trail for the distributor is one artefact
- You avoid the trap of updating the English and forgetting the German

Control the translation under your ISO 13485 document control (translation verification record, same revision and issue date as the English, same Basic UDI-DI / device list). If you're in several markets, the same logic applies market by market — Art. 19(4) is per-Member-State, so France, Italy, Spain etc. will each want their own, and a multilingual master gets unwieldy fast. At that point, separate per-language issues from a common controlled template is cleaner than one 8-language PDF.

I tried to look up the current text of the German implementing law to pin the citation exactly, but web access is disabled in this session — so below I'm clear about which parts are settled MDR text (high confidence) and which national detail you should verify before acting.

## Short answer

Yes, for Germany you should have a German-language Declaration of Conformity. But your distributor's framing ("everything has to be translated") is too broad — the correct rule is narrower and document-by-document.

## The legal chain

**MDR Art. 19(2)** is the operative provision. The DoC (content per Annex IV) must be drawn up in at least one official Union language, and then:

> "…shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available on the market."

So English-only is not inherently wrong — it's wrong *if a target Member State has required its own language*. This is a per-market question, and the answer for the Netherlands is not the answer for Germany.

**Germany has exercised that option.** The language rules sit in the MPDG (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz) — the Sprachenregelung provision, which I believe is § 9, though verify the section number and current wording. German is the required language for the market-facing documents. Practically, BfArM and the Länder authorities expect a German DoC, and this is what German distributors and notified bodies apply.

**Your distributor also has a direct stake.** Under Art. 14(2), a distributor must verify *before* making the device available that the DoC has been drawn up and that the required information is in the language Germany requires. Their own compliance is on the line, which is why they are pushing — not merely a preference.

## What actually needs German vs. what doesn't

| Document | German required for DE market? |
|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | Yes |
| Labelling / packaging | Yes |
| Instructions for use | Yes — but see the professional-use exception below |
| Technical documentation (Annex II/III) | Generally no — Germany accepts English for TD provided to authorities |
| Clinical evaluation report, PMS plan, PSUR | Generally no (they sit inside the TD) |
| QMS documents, internal SOPs | No |
| SSCP | N/A — Class IIa devices don't need one (implantable and Class III only) |

Two points that cut in your favour:

- **The DoC does not ship with each unit.** Art. 19(1) requires you to draw it up, keep it updated, and make it available to competent authorities. It is not required in the box for the end user. So "translating it for the German market" in practice means: a controlled German version you can hand to the distributor, the authority, or a tender body on request. It's a one-page document — this is not an expensive fight to concede.
- **MPDG allows an English IFU for devices supplied exclusively to professional users**, under conditions. If your Class IIa device is professional-use only, this exception may spare you the IFU translation — check the exact conditions, as this is the highest-value carve-out for you and it does *not* extend to the DoC.

## What I'd do

1. Issue a **bilingual EN/DE Declaration of Conformity** — single document, two columns or two pages — rather than two separate files. Mark English as the original/authoritative language and German as the translation. This avoids two documents drifting apart across revisions.
2. Bring the translation under **document control in your QMS**, with the translation regenerated on every DoC revision. A DoC whose German version states a stale classification, an outdated notified body certificate number, or a mismatched device description is itself a compliance defect — mistranslation here is a real risk, not a formality.
3. **Run the same Art. 19(2) analysis for your other markets** before the next audit. You will likely find you need more than English and German, and it's cheaper to do them in one batch.
4. Ask the distributor to **cite the specific MPDG provision** for anything beyond the DoC, labelling, and IFU. That's a reasonable request, it costs you nothing, and it will surface quickly whether their "everything" claim has substance behind it.

One caveat: I'm giving you the regulatory structure, not legal advice. Have your PRRC or German regulatory counsel confirm the current MPDG section text — particularly the professional-use IFU exception, since that's where the money is and where I'd least want you relying on my recollection.

graders.evidence:
Short answer: the DoC translation requirement is real, but it's set by Germany's national law — not by your distributor — and it's much narrower than "everything has to be in German."

I should flag upfront: I tried to check the current German text and web search is blocked in this session, so the Germany-specific point below is from my knowledge and worth verifying against the actual statute before you act on it.

## The legal basis

**MDR Article 19(2)** is the operative provision: the EU Declaration of Conformity "shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available."

So the obligation is conditional. There is no EU-wide rule that a DoC must be in every market's language — each Member State decides for its own territory. Your distributor is stating a conclusion that only the German legislator can supply.

For Germany, that determination sits in the **MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz), the national implementing act — the language provision is § 8. My recollection is that § 8 is directed at labelling, instructions for use and safety information rather than imposing a blanket German-language requirement on the DoC, and that English DoCs are commonly accepted in practice for the German market. I'd want you to confirm the current § 8 wording (or ask your Notified Body / a German regulatory counsel) rather than rely on that recollection — it's a one-paragraph check and it's the whole answer to your question.

## What does have to be in German

- **Labelling, IFU and safety information** (Annex I Section 23), under Art. 10(11). Germany requires German here. There is a narrow carve-out in the MPDG for devices intended exclusively for professional users, where another language may be acceptable — but it's conditional, and for a Class IIa device sold through a distributor I would not lean on it unless you've confirmed the conditions are met.
- **Field safety notices** and any safety communication to German users.
- **Implant card and patient information** (Art. 18), if applicable to your device.

## What does not

- **Technical documentation** does not have to be maintained in German. A competent authority can request specific documents in a language it accepts, but that's a request-driven obligation, not a standing translation duty.
- **Your QMS documentation**, internal procedures, clinical evaluation report, PSUR, and so on.

This is the part where your distributor is overreaching. "Everything has to be translated" is not the standard.

## Two practical points

**Just translate the DoC anyway.** It's an Annex IV document — one page: your name and SRN, Basic UDI-DI, product identification, device class, the conformity statement, the Notified Body name/number and certificate reference, place, date, signature. The cost of a certified German version is trivial next to the cost of arguing with a distributor about it or being wrong. Issue it as a bilingual or parallel German version, keep the English as the original, and control the version yourself so the two never drift apart.

**Don't let the distributor do the translating.** Under **Art. 16(2)(b)**, translating the information supplied with a device doesn't turn a distributor into a manufacturer — but it does trigger Art. 16(3) and (4): they need a quality management system covering translation accuracy, and they must notify you and the competent authority 28 days before making the relabelled device available. If they're pushing for German materials, the clean answer is that you supply them, under your own change control. That keeps the regulatory responsibility where it belongs and avoids a distributor-controlled translation of your IFU that you can't correct quickly.

If you can enable web search, I can pull the current § 8 MPDG text and confirm the DoC point directly.

to patients, never to home users. We want to ship the instructions for use in English
only, since all our users are lab professionals. Our German competitor does this. Can

**German market:** confirmed — device is made available in Germany, so MPDG applies.

**Answer:** No, not English *only*. § 8(2) sentence 2 lets you put the bulk of the IFU in English for an exclusively professional audience, but the **safety-related information must still be provided in German** (or the user's language), and you must have a *begründeter Fall* — so the realistic output is a bilingual/partly-German IFU, not an English-only one.

| Item | MDR/IVDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or English** — English alone is fine, no translation needed | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |
| Information for users (IFU, labelling) — default | not carried here | **German**, and it is a *condition of supply*: product may only be handed over if met | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 1 `[verified]` |
| Same, where audience is exclusively professional | not carried here | English or another easily understood language permitted — but only **in begründeten Fällen** | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2 `[verified]` |
| Safety-related information, even under that exception | not carried here | **German** or the user's language — the exception does not reach it | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2, final clause `[verified]` |

The exception is **cumulative**. All three must hold: (1) a justified case, (2) the information is *ausschließlich* for professional users, (3) safety-related information is still in German. Miss any one and sentence 1 snaps back — full German IFU, as a precondition of being allowed to supply the device at all.

Your facts get you condition (2) cleanly: hospital lab professionals only, never patients, never lay users. Condition (1) is a judgement you have to be able to justify and document. Condition (3) is the one that defeats "English only" outright — warnings, precautions, contraindications, biohazard and disposal handling, error/alarm states, anything the standard would treat as safety information needs a German version.

**On the competitor:** what a German competitor ships is not a compliance basis. They may have a documented justification you don't, they may be handling safety information in German in a way you can't see from the outside, or they may simply be non-compliant and not yet challenged. § 8(2) is a condition of supply — it doesn't get waived by market practice.

**What would change this:** if any part of the IFU is intended for a non-professional reader (a patient-facing result sheet, a sample-collection instruction that reaches a patient), sentence 1 applies to that part in full. Conversely, if the device is never made available in Germany, none of § 8 applies.

Two adjacent German duties worth flagging now rather than at recall time: if you ever run a field safety corrective action in Germany, the **FSN must be written in German** (§ 73(1) `[verified]`), and completion of an FSCA must be notified to both the competent authority and the federal higher authority (§ 73(2) `[verified]`) — so a German-language safety-communication capability is something you'll need regardless of how you resolve the IFU.

## Limits

> This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves, MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about France, Italy or elsewhere. A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

In particular, what counts as *sicherheitsbezogene Informationen* and what makes a *begründeter Fall* are not defined in § 8 — get that scoping decision reviewed by your regulatory lead before it goes into the technical documentation.

**German market:** confirmed — sold in Germany, so MPDG applies alongside IVDR
**Answer:** Not entirely. English-only IFU is permissible **only** if it is a *begründeter Fall*, the information is exclusively for professional users, **and** the safety-related information is still supplied in German — so a purely English document set does not comply.

| Item | MDR/IVDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or English** — English alone is fine, no translation needed | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |
| Information for users/patients (IFU, labelling) | not carried here | **German** by default, and it is a *condition of supply* — the product may only be handed over if met | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 1 `[verified]` |
| Same, professional users only | not carried here | English (or another easily understood language) permitted, but only in *begründeten Fällen* **and** where the information is **exclusively** for professional users | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 2 `[verified]` |
| Safety-related information | not carried here | **German** (or the user's language) even when the professional-user exception applies | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 2, final clause `[verified]` |
| Implant information (Art. 18(1) MDR) | not carried here | German, no exception — not applicable to your device | MPDG § 8(3) `[verified]` |

The three conditions in sentence 2 are cumulative. Miss any one and sentence 1 snaps back: full German.

Check that nothing in the accompanying information is directed at patients (e.g. result-interpretation leaflets meant to be handed on) and that your intended purpose does not admit self-testing or near-patient use by non-professionals. - **Default:** the Annex I Section 20 information must be in German.
- **Derogation:** for devices intended **exclusively for professional users**, the information may be in English (or another language easily understood by the user).
- **Carve-outs that survive the derogation:** safety-related information, and anything directed at patients, stays German.

1. **Declaration of conformity.** IVDR requires the DoC to be translated into the language(s) required by the Member State where the device is placed on market. Germany will want German. That's separate from the IFU derogation.
2. **Field safety notices.** Any FSN/FSCA to German users should be in German — BfArM will expect it, and this is exactly the moment where an English-only paper trail looks bad.
3. **Your distributor.** IVDR Art. 14 makes the distributor verify that the device is accompanied by the manufacturer's information in the language required by the Member State. Their own compliance check becomes your gate, and distributors are conservative here.

A benchtop analyser intended specifically for IVD procedures is almost certainly **Class A** under IVDR Annex VIII Rule 5 — self-declared, no notified body. Nobody reviews your labelling before market. The only check is Länder-level market surveillance, which is complaint-driven. So the competitor's practice tells you enforcement is unlikely; it tells you nothing about legality, and it isn't a defence if a lab or a competitor complains.

- **"Exclusively professional" has to be true in the technical file, not just in the sales channel.** If the intended purpose leaves room for near-patient testing, or the IFU doesn't clearly state professional-use-only, the derogation evaporates. - **The analyser may also be in Machinery scope.** The medical exclusion in machinery law is narrow (devices in direct contact with patients); a lab analyser typically isn't excluded, and lab instruments are commonly CE-marked under machinery law in parallel. **3. Germany's rule is § 11 MPDG.** The default is German. There is a derogation for devices supplied exclusively to professional users, under which the instructions for use may be in English. - Whether it covers only the **IFU** or also the **label/marking on the device**. Safety-relevant information and anything reaching patients typically stays German.

"All our users are lab professionals, therefore all our users read technical English" is an assumption that holds until the one MTA who doesn't causes a harm event. This is a separate and, in my view, larger exposure than the regulatory one.

**5. Parallel trade.** If a distributor resells into another member state, that state's language rules apply and most require the national language. Worth checking whether your distribution is genuinely Germany-only.

Not usable as evidence. Either they're relying on the same derogation (most likely), their device is classified differently, or they're non-compliant and nobody has looked yet. It also doesn't protect you: enforcement is per-manufacturer.

Ship English IFU under the professional-user derogation, but: keep safety-critical label content and FSNs in German, write the professional-users-only restriction into the intended purpose and the distribution contracts, and document the language decision in your technical file. Ship the **IFU in English**, plus **German labelling, warnings, and a German safety-information section/quick guide**, with the professional-user-only restriction hard-coded into the intended purpose and distribution agreements. You need the IFU in **Castilian Spanish** and **European Portuguese**. Nothing more, and no German — the MPDG language rules attach to devices made available on the German market, which you aren't doing.

## The EU layer

MDR Article 10(11): the manufacturer must ensure the device is accompanied by the Annex I Section 23 information "in an official Union language(s) **determined by the Member State in which the device is made available to the user or patient**."

Two consequences worth internalising:

- **The trigger is where the device reaches the user, not where you ship.** If your Spanish distributor onward-sells into France or Germany, a new language obligation arises there, and that entity picks up importer/distributor duties. Worth a contractual restriction in your distribution agreements if you genuinely want to stay two-market.
- **Your distributors will police this.** Article 14(2)(b) requires a distributor to verify, before making the device available, that it carries the Article 10(11) information in the required languages. Expect Spanish and Portuguese distributors to reject non-compliant stock.

Language obligations are class-independent. What Class IIb *does* change: the Annex I carve-out permitting the IFU to be omitted or abridged applies only to Class I and IIa devices. For IIb, a full IFU is mandatory, so there's no path to reducing translation scope that way.

## Spain

The operative national instrument is **Real Decreto 192/2023, de 21 de marzo**, which replaced RD 1591/2009.

The substantive rule, carried forward from RD 1591/2009 Art. 4.6: label particulars and IFU for devices supplied to the **final user must be at least in the official Spanish language of the State (Castilian) — regardless of whether the device is for professional use or not.** This is the point people get wrong. Several Member States relax the requirement for professional-use-only devices; Spain historically has not. Do not assume a "professional use only, English is fine" argument works here.

Two things to verify in the RD 192/2023 text rather than take from me: the exact article number, and whether the 2023 recast introduced any professional-use flexibility that didn't exist under the 2009 decree. I have low confidence there is one, but it's the single question that would most change your translation budget.

**Co-official languages.** State-level medical device law requires Castilian only. However, Catalonia's consumer code (Llei 22/2010, Codi de consum) requires that information for products distributed to consumers in Catalonia be available in Catalan. If your IIb device is professional-use-only in a clinical setting, this is a low practical risk. If it's lay-use or home-use, get local advice — this is a real enforcement surface and it's a consumer-law regulator, not AEMPS.

## Portugal

Requirement: **European Portuguese (pt-PT)**, for devices reaching the final user. Do not accept a Brazilian Portuguese translation from a vendor — terminology and orthography differ, and INFARMED-facing documents are expected in pt-PT.

Under the old DL 145/2009 (Art. 7), the rule was Portuguese for anything reaching the final user, with a discretionary power for INFARMED to authorise another language for exclusively professional-use devices. **Whether that discretionary carve-out survives into Portugal's MDR implementing decree-law is the thing to check** — and note it was a permission you had to apply for, not a self-assessed exemption, so it was rarely worth using.

- **Label** — same Article 10(11) rule. Symbols per EN ISO 15223-1:2021 carry a lot of label content language-free, which genuinely reduces label translation work, but they don't substitute for required narrative text.

If you were planning eIFU under Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 to avoid printing two language versions: eligibility is narrow. Check whether the current text carries any relaxation for devices used **exclusively by healthcare professionals** — the predecessor decree was strict, and I'd want the live article text before relying on any carve-out.
2. **Portugal** — the MDR implementing decree-law (successor to DL 145/2009) similarly requires Portuguese. Historically Portugal was somewhat more permissive for professional-use-only devices than Spain. Confirm with INFARMED, ideally in writing, if you intend to rely on that.

If your device ever reaches a lay user or patient, treat national language as mandatory in both markets with no carve-out available. That's the safe design assumption, and the reason most manufacturers just translate both rather than litigate the professional-use question.

**On Spain's co-official languages:** the medical-device requirement is Castilian. Catalan, Galician, Basque and Valencian are not required for device IFU under the state medical-device rules. Regional consumer-protection statutes occasionally get raised in this context but do not extend to MDR device information.

## Electronic IFU doesn't reduce this

Under Regulation (EU) 2021/2226, eIFU is available only for specific categories — implantables, fixed installed devices, devices with a built-in display, and software — and only for **professional** users. Even where you qualify:

- the website must carry the IFU **in the languages determined by each Member State** where the device is made available, so you still need Spanish and Portuguese;
- you must supply a paper IFU free of charge on request, within 7 calendar days.

eIFU changes the delivery mechanism, not the language obligation.

## Adjacent obligations people forget

- **Declaration of Conformity (Art. 19)**: must be translated into the language(s) required by each Member State where the device is made available — so Spanish and Portuguese versions, not just English.
- **Field safety notices (Art. 89)**: must be in the language(s) accepted by each Member State. Build Spanish/Portuguese FSN templates *now*, not during a recall.
- **Implant card (Art. 18)** — only if your Class IIb device is implantable: card and accompanying information in the language determined by each Member State.
- **Distributor-performed translations (Art. 16)**: if a local Spanish or Portuguese distributor translates your IFU, that alone doesn't make them a manufacturer — but they must operate a QMS covering translation accuracy and notify you before making the translated device available. If you're using distributor translations, get this into your distribution agreements and audit it; a bad translation remains your safety problem.

One flag on scope: "Spain and Portugal only" is a commercial intention, not a regulatory boundary. Once CE-marked, the device is legally free-moving across the EEA, and parallel distribution into another Member State can pull you into that state's language rules. Worth a line in your PMS plan rather than a surprise later.

Portuguese is required for labelling and IFU. The historic basis was Decreto-Lei 145/2009 art. 6; the MDR-era implementing decree-law supersedes it — verify the current instrument and article number.

Portugal has historically allowed English for **exclusively professional-use** devices, in practice subject to INFARMED's position. Again: confirm rather than assume, and note that even where English is tolerated, §23.1(d) comprehensibility still binds you.

Correct — no German. The obligation attaches per Member State where *you* make the device available. Two caveats:

1. **Onward movement.** Goods circulate freely in the EU. If a distributor or parallel trader moves your Spanish/Portuguese-only stock into Germany, *they* become responsible under Art. 16(2)–(4): translating the IFU is a permitted repackaging-type activity, but it triggers a QMS covering translation accuracy, notification to the competent authority and your notified body, and 28-day notice. Worth an explicit contractual term with your distributors.
2. If you later add Germany, German becomes mandatory for both professional and lay devices — Germany allows no professional-use English carve-out.

## Don't forget the adjacent documents

The IFU is not the only thing carrying a language obligation:

- **The label itself** — same rule as the IFU. ISO 15223-1 symbols reduce but do not eliminate the burden.
- **Declaration of conformity** (Art. 19 / Annex IV) — must be translated into the language(s) required by each Member State where the device is made available. In practice: ES and PT.
- **If your IIb device is implantable** — the Art. 18 implant card and accompanying patient information must be in the national language(s) of each Member State, and an Art. 32 SSCP is required (notified-body-validated in English; you supply the ES/PT translations, and the language set must be declared in the technical documentation).
- **Field safety notices** (Art. 89) — national languages, so you need translation capacity standing by, not just at launch.

## eIFU

Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 lets you replace paper IFU with electronic ones, but only for defined categories — essentially **professional-use** devices, fixed installed devices, and implantables/software in narrow cases. It does not reduce the *language* set: the website must carry every required language for every Member State of supply, and you must ship paper on request free of charge within 7 days (or before the procedure, for planned use). A Class IIb device intended for lay users cannot use eIFU.

## The one thing that determines your answer

**Is the device intended exclusively for healthcare professionals, or for lay/patient use?** That single fact decides whether the ES/PT professional-use flexibilities are even available to you.

My recommendation regardless: produce a single multilingual IFU in Spanish and Portuguese. The professional-use English carve-outs are narrow, nationally variable, and can be withdrawn or reinterpreted; the cost delta of a two-language booklet over an English one is small compared to a relabelling exercise mid-market. Reserve the flexibility argument for a fallback if a translation slips, not as the launch plan.

The same language determination attaches to:

- **Label and packaging text** — same Art. 10(11) obligation, same languages.
- **EU Declaration of Conformity** — Art. 19 requires translation into the language(s) required by the Member States where the device is made available. ES and PT here.

So the below is from knowledge. I've marked the items where you should confirm the exact § number or figure against the current text before relying on it — the MDR-derived clocks I'm confident in; the German § numbering is where memory is most likely to drift. This is regulatory orientation, not legal advice.

## What regime you're in

An unapproved (non-CE-marked) Class III device investigated to demonstrate conformity is an **Article 62 MDR** clinical investigation. In Germany that means a **dual requirement** — you need *both*:

1. a **zustimmende Bewertung** (favourable opinion) from a **registered ethics committee**, and
2. a **Genehmigung** (authorisation) from the **Bundesoberbehörde** — BfArM by default, PEI if the device incorporates a substance derived from human blood/plasma or otherwise falls in PEI's remit.

There is **no tacit approval** for this class. Silence does not let you start.

Procedurally it is a **single, coordinated submission**: you file one dossier via **DMIDS** (the German medical device information and database system, run by BfArM), and BfArM routes it to the ethics committee. The EK and the Bundesoberbehörde then run on one shared clock rather than two sequential ones. The EUDAMED clinical investigation module is not the mandatory route yet, so DMIDS is the filing channel.

## Ethics committee submission content

The core dossier is **MDR Annex XV, Chapter II** — that is the master checklist, and the EK sees essentially the full application, not a reduced set. What the EK assesses in its own right (per MDR Art. 62(4) letters b, c, d, f, h, l, plus the German special-population rules):

**Scientific / technical**
- Clinical Investigation Plan (CIP) per Annex XV Ch. II §3
- Investigator's Brochure
- Risk–benefit analysis and risk management documentation
- Pre-clinical data: biocompatibility, sterilisation validation, electrical safety/EMC, software V&V, animal data as applicable
- Manufacturer's declaration that the device conforms to the **Annex I GSPRs apart from the aspects under investigation**, and that every precaution has been taken to protect subjects
- Statistical rationale and justification of the sample size

**Subject protection — this is where German committees are strictest**
- **Patienteninformation and Einwilligungserklärung, in German**, separate versions per subject group
- Subject **insurance (Probandenversicherung)** — MDR Art. 69 requires a compensation system; MPDG sets a hard minimum sum insured per subject (my recollection is **€500,000 per subject**, carried over from the old MPG regime — verify the current figure and the § before you bind cover). Provide the insurance certificate with the submission; committees routinely reject on inadequate or missing cover.
- Data protection concept under GDPR/BDSG, including the legal basis for processing health data and the retention/deletion plan
- Recruitment materials and any subject compensation/expense arrangements
- Documentation for special groups if applicable — minors, incapacitated adults, pregnant/breastfeeding women, emergency situations each have their own MPDG conditions (the §§ in the mid-20s range; check the numbering) and the EK verifies these specifically

**Suitability**
- CVs and qualification evidence for the **Prüfer** — MPDG imposes a minimum practical experience requirement for investigators (I recall **two years** of clinical investigation experience; confirm)
- Site suitability declarations (Geeignetheit der Prüfstelle) for each centre
- Financial arrangements, including investigator/sponsor financial interests

**Formalities**
- Sponsor's EU establishment or designated legal representative in the EU
- EK fee under the relevant Land's fee schedule, plus the separate BfArM fee
- Language: German is mandatory for all subject-facing documents; parts of the technical dossier are generally acceptable in English — confirm with the specific EK, practice varies

One structural point worth knowing if you ran trials under the old MPG: for **multicentre** investigations there is now a **single ethics committee opinion covering all sites**. No per-site local votes.

## Deadlines

| Step | Clock | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Validation (in scope + complete) | **10 days** from receipt; you get a single ID number | MDR Art. 70(1)–(4) |
| If deficiencies found | You respond within **max 10 days**; authority then re-validates within **5 days**. No response → application **lapses** | MDR Art. 70(3) |
| EK opinion + authorisation decision | **45 days** from the **validation date** | MDR Art. 70(7)(b) |
| Extension for expert consultation | **+20 days** | MDR Art. 70(7)(b) |
| Requests for information (Nachforderung) | Clock is **suspended** while you respond; the authority sets the response period | MPDG (verify § and whether RFI is limited to one round) |
| Start of investigation | Only after **both** positive EK opinion **and** express BfArM/PEI authorisation | — |
| Substantial modification | Notify; may implement **no earlier than 38 days** after notification, absent objection | MDR Art. 75(3) |
| Serious incident with imminent risk of death/serious deterioration | Report **immediately, ≤2 calendar days** from awareness | MDR Art. 80(2) |
| Death or unanticipated serious deterioration | **≤7 calendar days** | MDR Art. 80(3) |
| End of investigation | Notify within **15 days** | MDR Art. 77(1) |
| Temporary halt / early termination | **15 days**; **24 hours** if halted on safety grounds | MDR Art. 77(2) |
| Final clinical investigation report | **1 year** after end; **3 months** after early termination | MDR Art. 77(5) |

So the realistic planning figure from validated submission to a decision is **45 days, or 65 with the expert extension** — plus however long your own RFI responses take, since that time is yours, not the clock's. Budget 3–4 months from filing to first subject in as a working assumption.

## Two things to check before you file

- **Which ethics committee.** It must be a **registered** EK under MPDG (BfArM maintains the register). The rule allocating the competent EK is not free choice in the way sponsors sometimes assume — confirm the allocation rule and whether the choice is yours or determined by the coordinating investigator's site.
- **BfArM vs. PEI.** If there is any blood/plasma-derived or tissue component, competence shifts to PEI and the contact points change.

## The regulatory frame

An unapproved (non-CE-marked) Class III device studied to generate data for conformity assessment is an **Article 62 MDR** clinical investigation. Germany layers the MPDG (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz) and the MPKPV (Medizinprodukte-Klinische-Prüfungen-Verordnung) on top of MDR Arts. 62–82 and Annex XV.

**Dual gate — both required before first subject in:**

1. **Authorization (Genehmigung) by the Bundesoberbehörde** — BfArM in the normal case; **Paul-Ehrlich-Institut** if the device incorporates as an integral part a medicinal substance derived from human blood or plasma, or otherwise falls in PEI's remit.
2. **Favourable opinion (zustimmende Bewertung) of a registered ethics committee.**

For Class III there is **no tacit approval**. MDR Art. 70(7)(b) requires an explicit authorization notification — the "start after validation" shortcut applies only to Class I and non-invasive IIa/IIb.

**Submission channel:** one electronic application via **DMIDS** covering both the authority and the EC; the two assessments run coordinated and in parallel. (EUDAMED's clinical investigation module is being phased in under Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 — confirm the current mandatory-use status, this has been moving.)

**Ethics committee:** must be an EC constituted under Landesrecht **and registered with BfArM** under the MPDG. One EC opinion covers all German sites — no per-site votes as under the old MPG.

## What the EC submission must contain

The core is **MDR Annex XV, Chapter II**, plus MPDG-specific additions. The EC's remit is the ethical/subject-protection half of the dossier (BfArM takes device safety and performance), but the EC receives the full package:

**Annex XV Chapter II baseline**
- Application form and cover letter; the single identification number for the investigation
- **Clinical Investigation Plan (CIP)** per Annex XV Ch. II §3 — objectives, endpoints, statistical design and justification of sample size, risk mitigation, subject withdrawal, monitoring plan
- **Investigator's Brochure**
- Device description, manufacturing/sterilization information, preclinical and bench data, biocompatibility
- **Risk–benefit analysis** and risk management file per ISO 14971
- Declaration that the device conforms to the Annex I GSPRs apart from the aspects under investigation
- Justification of the design's suitability for the intended purpose

**Subject-protection documents (the EC's main focus)**
- **Patient information and informed consent forms, in German** — including data protection information
- Recruitment material (adverts, screening scripts)
- Arrangements for compensation of subjects, and for investigator remuneration
- Provisions for vulnerable subjects, if applicable — Germany imposes **stricter national conditions than the MDR baseline** for minors, incapacitated adults, pregnant/nursing women and emergency enrolment. If your protocol touches any of these, treat it as the highest-risk part of the submission.

**German-specific additions**
- **Probandenversicherung (subject insurance) certificate** — mandatory, with a statutory minimum sum insured per subject. I recall €500,000 per subject; **verify the current figure**, and confirm the policy covers all German sites and the full follow-up period.
- **Data protection concept** under GDPR/BDSG
- **Investigator and site suitability** — CVs, ISO 14155/GCP training records, site declarations (Prüfstellenerklärungen)
- **Site contracts** (Prüfstellenverträge) between sponsor and institutions
- Proof of **fee payment** — separate BfArM and EC fees

## Deadlines

**Firm (MDR Art. 70, applies directly in Germany):**

| Step | Clock |
|---|---|
| Validation — sponsor notified whether in scope and complete | **10 days** from receipt |
| Sponsor response if incomplete | **max 10 days** |
| Re-validation after response | **5 days** |
| Assessment / authorization decision, Class III | **45 days** from the validation date |
| Extension for expert consultation | **+20 days** → **65 days max** |

The **validation date**, not the submission date, starts the 45-day clock. Requests for clarification stop the clock. A negative EC opinion blocks the start irrespective of what BfArM decides.

**Firm post-approval obligations:**
- **Substantial modifications** (Art. 75): may be implemented **no earlier than 38 days** after notification, absent objection from BfArM or the EC.
- **SAE reporting** (Art. 80): death or unanticipated serious deterioration in health — **immediately, no later than 2 calendar days**; other SAEs and device deficiencies that could have led to one — **immediately, no later than 7 calendar days**.
- **End of investigation** (Art. 77): notify within **15 days**; temporary halt or early termination **for safety reasons within 24 hours**.
- **Clinical investigation report**: within **1 year** of end of investigation, or **3 months** of early termination.

**Verify these:** the MPKPV sets *intermediate* German milestones — by which day the EC must deliver its assessment to BfArM so the coordinated decision lands inside the 45 days, and how the EC's own clarification round is sequenced. I do not have those numbers reliably, and they are exactly the ones that drive your submission planning. Get them from the MPKPV text and your chosen EC's published Verfahrensordnung.

## Two things that commonly derail the timeline

1. **Ionizing radiation.** If the investigation involves X-ray or radioactive procedures beyond standard of care, you need a **separate approval under the Strahlenschutzgesetz (§ 31 ff. StrlSchG)** from BfS. It runs on its own clock and is frequently the critical path — start it in parallel, not after.
2. **Section numbering.** I'm confident on the substance above, but **not on the specific MPDG § numbers** for the EC provisions (the clinical investigation sections sit roughly in §§ 24–47). Pull the current consolidated text rather than citing from a summary.

## The basic structure

A Class III device without a CE mark, investigated to generate data for conformity assessment, is an **Article 62 MDR clinical investigation**. Germany layers the MPDG (in force 26 May 2021, replacing the MPG) on top, and the key German-specific point is:

**You need two things, not one.** Unlike some Member States, Germany requires *both*:
1. **Genehmigung** (authorization) from the Bundesoberbehörde — BfArM, or **PEI** if your device incorporates a substance derived from human blood or plasma, or is used in combination with certain biologics; and
2. **Zustimmende Bewertung** (favourable opinion) from a **registered ethics committee** (*registrierte Ethik-Kommission*).

BfArM cannot issue the authorization without the favourable EK opinion. There is **no tacit approval** for Class III — MDR Art. 70(7)(b) tacit start applies only to Class I and non-invasive IIa/IIb.

**One submission, parallel assessment.** You file a single dossier through **DMIDS** (Deutsches Medizinprodukteinformations- und Datenbanksystem); BfArM and the EK assess in parallel on a coordinated clock. For multi-centre investigations, MPDG moved to a **single lead EK opinion** covering all German sites — no separate local votes, unlike the old MPG regime. The competent EK is normally the one at the *Leiter der klinischen Prüfung*'s institution (Landesärztekammer or medical faculty EK), and it must appear on BfArM's published register.

⚠️ **Check the Eudamed transition.** Regulation (EU) 2024/1860 phases in mandatory Eudamed modules; the clinical investigations module was scheduled to become mandatory around late 2026/2027, which would change the filing route away from DMIDS. Confirm current status with BfArM before you file.

## What the EK dossier must contain

The substantive content is **MDR Annex XV, Chapter II** — MPDG adds German procedural and protective requirements on top.

**Core documents**
- Application form and single identification number; sponsor details, plus **EU-established legal representative** if the sponsor is outside the EU (Art. 62(2))
- **Investigator's Brochure** (Annex XV Ch. II §2)
- **Clinical Investigation Plan** per Annex XV Ch. II §3, written to **ISO 14155:2020**
- **Manufacturer's signed statement** that the device conforms to the Annex I GSPRs apart from the aspects under investigation, and that all precautions have been taken

**Ethics-specific**
- Subject information sheet and informed consent form — **in German**
- Justification and specific safeguards for **vulnerable subjects** — MPDG contains its own provisions (stricter than MDR Arts. 64–68) for minors, persons incapable of consenting, pregnant and nursing women, and emergency situations. For a Class III device these are frequently the sticking point; if any of these groups are in scope, budget extra review time.
- Recruitment materials, subject compensation arrangements
- Data protection: GDPR + BDSG §27, and a DPIA where required
- Investigator CVs and evidence of **site suitability** (*Eignung der Prüfstelle*). The *Leiter der klinischen Prüfung* must be a physician with appropriate qualification; MPDG carries over the MPG expectation of **at least two years' experience in clinical investigations of medical devices**.
- Sponsor–site contracts, financing disclosure

**Insurance (Probandenversicherung)** — mandatory, and a hard blocker if wrong. The figure carried over from MPG §20(3) is **€500,000 per subject** for death or permanent incapacity. Verify the current statutory minimum in MPDG; the certificate must name the investigation and the German sites.

**Class III technical evidence** — biocompatibility, sterility, electrical safety, bench verification/validation, animal data where applicable, the clinical evaluation report and literature, and the risk management file with the benefit–risk analysis.

**Language:** patient-facing documents in German, non-negotiable. Most EKs want the core dossier in German; BfArM and some EKs will accept English for the IB and technical annexes — confirm with your specific EK in advance.

## Deadlines

**Getting in (MDR Art. 70):**

| Step | Clock |
|---|---|
| Validation notice from authority | **10 days** from receipt; silence = deemed validated |
| Sponsor completes a deficient application | **10 days** max, or the application **lapses** |
| Re-validation after sponsor response | 5 further days |
| Decision, Class III | **45 days** from validation date |
| Extension for expert consultation | **+20 days** → 65 days max |
| Requests for information | Clock **suspends** from request until you respond |

Realistic planning: **~55–65 days** from validation to decision, plus your own turnaround on questions. Front-load the EK's likely queries — clock-stops are where these timelines actually slip.

**During the investigation:**

| Event | Deadline |
|---|---|
| Substantial modification (Art. 75) | Notify both BfArM and EK; may implement no earlier than **38 days** after notification, absent objection |
| Death or unanticipated serious deterioration | **2 calendar days** from awareness |
| Other SAEs with causal relationship, device deficiencies that could have led to an SAE, new findings | **7 calendar days** (Art. 80, per MDCG 2020-10/1) |
| Annual safety report | Yearly, for the duration |

**Ending it (Art. 77):**

| Event | Deadline |
|---|---|
| End of investigation in Germany | **15 days** |
| Early termination or temporary halt | **15 days** |
| …if for **safety reasons** | **24 hours** |
| Clinical investigation report + lay summary | **1 year** after end; **3 months** after early termination |

## Practical notes

- **Fees are separate and additive** — a BfArM authorization fee plus the EK's own fee (typically low-to-mid four figures). Budget both.
- **Talk to BfArM early.** A scientific advice meeting before filing is worth it for an unapproved Class III device, particularly on the adequacy of preclinical data and the endpoint design.
- **Pick your EK before you write the dossier.** Registered EKs publish their own submission forms, formatting rules and language policies, and these vary. Working backwards from your chosen EK's checklist avoids a validation-stage bounce.

Sources unavailable this session — I'd recommend confirming against gesetze-im-internet.de/mpdg and BfArM's clinical investigations guidance, especially the MPDG § numbers, the insurance minimum, and the current DMIDS/Eudamed filing route. **German market:** confirmed — devices affected in Germany

**What would change this:** if Germany turns out not to be among the affected markets — if no affected device was made available there — § 73(1) does not bite and English-only is not a German problem.

## The language problem

MDR (Regulation (EU) 2017/745) Article 89(8) requires that the Field Safety Notice be drafted in **the official Union language(s) determined by the Member State in which the FSCA is taking place**. This is not the manufacturer's choice, and it's separate from your labelling/IFU language obligations under Article 10(11).

- **Germany: German is required.** BfArM will expect a German-language "Kundeninformation"/FSN, and it publishes FSNs in German. No exception for professional-only devices.
- **Every other affected Member State needs its own accepted language** — French for France, Italian for Italy, Spanish for Spain, Polish for Poland, etc.
- **English is only sufficient in a few places** — Ireland and Malta, plus (in practice, and only for some device/user categories) a handful of Nordic/Benelux authorities. Don't assume; check each affected authority's published requirement rather than relying on a general "English is fine for professionals" belief.
- The translation obligation covers the **whole package**: the FSN body, the acknowledgement/reply form, and any attached user instructions, diagrams, or quarantine labels. A German FSN with an English reply form will get pushed back.

Practical note: translate from a single locked master English version, keep the master and every translation under the same document/version number, and have the translations reviewed by someone with device-regulatory literacy in that language — mistranslating the required action or the residual risk is a vigilance finding in its own right.

## Other things worth checking before it goes out

**Submit to the authorities in advance.** Article 89(8) requires the FSN to be submitted to the relevant competent authorities *before* it is distributed to users, except in cases of urgency. Several authorities, BfArM included, will comment on wording. Distributing first and notifying after is a common and avoidable finding.

**Report the FSCA itself.** Separate from the FSN, the FSCA must be reported under Article 87(1)(b) to the competent authorities of all affected Member States, including any FSCA you're running in a third country if the underlying reason isn't confined to that market.

**Coordinating competent authority.** As a US manufacturer with no EU registered place of business, your coordinating competent authority under Article 89(9) will normally be the authority of the Member State where your authorised representative is established — i.e. **HPRA in Ireland**. That doesn't relieve you of notifying each affected Member State; it determines who coordinates the assessment.

**Your Irish AR is in the loop by law.** Under Article 11 the AR must cooperate with competent authorities, hold the technical documentation, and act as the contact point. Check your mandate: it should say explicitly who submits vigilance reports and FSNs, and the AR should be receiving copies of all of it. Also confirm your PRRC-equivalent sign-off path.

**FSN content and form.** Use the harmonised FSN template and content expected by the MDCG vigilance guidance (MDCG 2023-3, carrying forward the old MEDDEV 2.12-1 structure): device identification including UDI-DI/models/lot ranges, description of the problem and the risk, the specific action required of the user with a deadline, what the manufacturer will do, an acknowledgement mechanism, a named contact, and an explicit statement that the relevant national competent authority has been informed.

**Distribution and effectiveness.** Reach all users and economic operators actually holding affected devices — not just your direct customers; distributors and importers have their own onward-notification duties under Articles 13 and 14. Track acknowledgements, chase non-responders, and plan the effectiveness check, since authorities will ask for completion data.

**Eudamed.** My information on the mandatory-use timeline runs to mid-2026, and the vigilance module was on a later rollout track than actor/UDI/certificates. Confirm the current status before assuming national channels (MIR/FSCA forms to each authority) are still the route — if the vigilance module has become mandatory, submission mechanics change even though none of the substantive obligations above do.

**Scope beyond the EU.** If affected devices went to Great Britain, Northern Ireland, Switzerland, or Turkey, those are separate reporting regimes with their own language and notification rules.

I'd hold distribution until the German and other required translations are ready and the advance submissions to BfArM, HPRA, and the other affected authorities have gone in — unless the risk is urgent enough that delay is itself the greater hazard, in which case distribute and notify simultaneously, and document that urgency rationale.

## The language requirement

MDR Article 89(8) is explicit: the field safety notice "shall be edited in an official Union language or languages determined by the Member State in which the field safety corrective action is being taken." Language is not the manufacturer's choice — it's each destination Member State's choice.

Practically:

- **Ireland, Malta**: English is fine.
- **France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Poland, etc.**: national language.
- **Netherlands and the Nordics**: often accept English *where the device is used exclusively by healthcare professionals* — but confirm per country rather than assuming. This is worth checking before you pay for 20 translations you don't need.
- **Belgium**: depends on region (NL/FR/DE).

Same rule applies to everything in the package the user actually has to read and act on — the acknowledgement/reply form, any return instructions, quarantine labels. A German FSN with an English reply form is a common finding.

## Other things I'd check on this action

**Notify the authorities before you distribute.** Under Art. 89(8) you report the FSCA to the competent authority of every Member State where the action is being carried out, and except in urgent cases the CAs get the opportunity to comment on the draft FSN. Distributing first and notifying after is the second-most-common problem after language. Your coordinating competent authority is most likely the HPRA (Ireland), since that's where your authorised representative is established — but you still report to each affected national authority.

**Your Irish AR has independent duties.** Article 11(3) obliges the AR to cooperate with competent authorities on preventive/corrective action and to forward information. Make sure they're actually looped in as a party to the action, not just cc'd — and that they hold a copy of the FSCA file, since authorities may go to them first.

**Use the MDCG FSN template** (MDCG 2023-3 carries the current template and vigilance Q&A). It maps directly onto the Art. 89(8) content requirements: unambiguous device identification including UDI-DIs, manufacturer identification, a clear statement of the reason and the risk *without understating it*, and an explicit list of actions the user must take.

**Translation control.** You remain responsible for translation accuracy — this is a QMS-controlled document, not a machine-translation job. Keep the English master, version-control each translation, and retain them in the vigilance file.

**Eudamed.** Reporting of vigilance/FSCA through Eudamed was being phased to mandatory use under Regulation (EU) 2024/1860, with the vigilance module scheduled after the actor/UDI/certificate modules. That timeline sat just past what I can verify — check the current status of the vigilance module before you decide between Eudamed submission and national portals, because it may now be mandatory rather than voluntary.

**Scope check.** "Several EU countries" — confirm whether affected devices also went to Switzerland (CH-REP, and German/French/Italian), the UK (MHRA, separate regime and separate reporting), or Norway/Iceland/Liechtenstein. Hold distribution to Germany and the other non-English-language markets, get the FSN into the MDCG template if it isn't already, submit the draft to the affected CAs (coordinating through HPRA), and commission controlled translations for the markets that require them. Ireland and any other English-accepting markets can proceed once the CAs have had their look at the draft.

For Germany that means **German**. BfArM will expect a German FSN, and distributors/users there can reasonably refuse to act on an English one. Same logic applies country-by-country across your affected markets:

- **Local language effectively mandatory:** Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Poland, and most others.
- **Belgium:** Dutch and French (German too, depending on the region served).
- **Sometimes accept English for professional-use devices:** Ireland, Malta, Netherlands, and the Nordics — but this is a per-authority position, not a rule, and it should be confirmed with each CA rather than assumed.
- **Lay/patient users:** local language, in lay-understandable terms, essentially everywhere — including in the countries that tolerate English for HCP-only devices.

Verify the current position on the relevant national competent authority websites for each affected Member State; requirements do shift.

## Two other things to get right before distribution

**1. Submit the draft to the coordinating competent authority first.** Article 89(8) requires you to give the coordinating CA the draft FSN before you send it, so it can comment — the only exception is genuine urgency. Since you're a non-EU manufacturer, the coordinating CA will normally be the authority of the Member State where your authorised representative sits, i.e. **HPRA in Ireland**, though the CAs can agree otherwise for a multi-country action. If you've already started distributing, tell HPRA now.

**2. Confirm the FSCA itself was reported.** Article 87(1)(b) requires reporting any FSCA on Union-market devices, including one triggered by action taken in the US. Also confirm which channel applies right now — Eudamed's vigilance module has been phased in on a different timeline from the actor/UDI/certificate modules, and several Member States still take reports through national portals. My information here runs to May 2026, so check the current status rather than relying on that.

## Also worth a quick check

- **FSN content:** unique reference number and date, device identification including Basic UDI-DI/UDI-DI, affected lot/serial ranges, the hazard and clinical risk, the specific action the recipient must take, a statement that the competent authorities have been informed, and an acknowledgement/reply form. Follow the MDCG FSN template.
- **Translation quality:** these are safety-critical texts. Use qualified translation with review, and keep the English master version referenced by the same FSN number so the versions stay traceable to each other.
- **Effectiveness tracking:** you need returned acknowledgements and a way to demonstrate the FSCA actually reached users — that's much harder to defend if recipients couldn't read the notice.
- **Non-EU markets:** if the same devices went to Great Britain or Switzerland, those are separate regimes (MHRA; Swissmedic with a CH-REP and DE/FR/IT notices) and aren't covered by the EU filing.
- **Your Irish AR** has its own Article 11 duties to cooperate on corrective actions — loop them in as the coordinating point rather than after the fact.
